title: aMindLikeARazor
text:
Preface
The CEO of a popular razor-making company is being interviewed by a famous business magazine. “Is it hard to recruit the best minds to work for you?” asks the interviewer. “Well,” says the CEO, “our people could have worked for NASA or Ferrari. But when we tell them that they will be working on the interaction between living biological tissue and the sharpest object known to man, we have no problem getting them to sign up.”1
Economics is about the interaction between the sharpest known object – your razor-like intelligence, the sharpest logic, the glint of mathematical steel – and the living, breathing, pulsating ordinary business of life. We answer questions like: what makes some countries rich and others poor? Why do we fall into high unemployment, and how do we get out of it? Why do financial crises always seem to catch us by surprise? Why are things so expensive and who’s to blame and who’s in charge? How does our country interact with the rest of the world? What determines prices and why do they change? Why does the free market work so well so much of the time, delivering trillions of dollars of goods and services without a glitch and without a massive coordinating plan? How do monopoly power or information failure mess up that beautiful thing? How do we make it work when what you do affects me? What does economics have to say about seemingly uneconomic subjects, like the family or people’s work?
This is an Economics book. This means that you should be ready to work hard, and have fun working hard. It’s written so that introductory students can get all they need – and if they want to learn more, the intermediate and advanced topics are right there. And it is written so that intermediate-level students can easily go back to the topics they (of course) learned and almost remember but just need a refresher for. It’s written for beginning students who remember their Algebra II, for intermediate students who loved their Pre-Calculus, and for more advanced students who think better when they take derivatives and maximize.
To learn more about Quarto books visit https://quarto.org/docs/books.

title: 1  The Macroeconomic Perspective
text:
1.1 Reading
You work hard, develop useful skills, and make careful financial decisions. What important things about your economic future are still outside your individual control? The opportunities to earn may be abundant or scarce. Your earnings may be able to buy all you need or leave you short. The economy may offer little, or may have a great deal available.
What are the conditions that shape those opportunities? How do our decisions collectively help create those conditions?
Read these short pieces before reading the rest of the chapter:
Microeconomics is about individual decisions. Macroeconomics is about how those individual decisions lead to outcomes for all of us. Micro individual decisions are made with constraints and in response to incentives. Macro context is about how those constraints come about and how those incentives interact.
The macro perspective is about feedback. Once you zoom out of individual decisions, you see that these interactions lead to big-picture thinking.
The macro perspective is also about the common good, about what is good for all of us together. Micro decisions are about what is good for us, individually, which can be added up. But macroeconomics is about the institutions, preconditions, and outcomes that are good because they are shared and that can only be enjoyed in common. Prosperity, stability, dynamism, predictability; opportunities and infrastructure; the availability of resources to adapt to change and the willingness to counteract nasty shocks: these topics are the bread and butter of macroeconomics, and they necessarily involve going beyond “each one of us, separately” and ask us to think about “all of us, together.”
In Macroeconomics, we focus on questions like:
You want to know what opportunities are available to you. Your parents want to know what opportunities will be available to their children. Your job outlook depends on where and when you are looking. Will next year’s raise actually let you buy more? Why does the economic situation change, and can we do something about it?

title: 1  The Macroeconomic Perspective
text:
IMF / Finance & Development, “Gross Domestic Product: An Economy’s All.” What is one reason to care about GDP growth, and one reason GDP cannot tell us everything we want to know?
Vermann, Katarina (2012) “Wait, Is Saving Good or Bad? The Paradox of Thrift.” How could cutting spending help one household but create difficulties if many households do it simultaneously? (Careful: this is about the short-run effect, not about the long-run impact of saving.)
Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (2025) “The Differences between Prices and Inflation Explained.” Can inflation fall while the cost of living continues to rise? Explain without using a formula.




Often, the individually rational decision depends on everyone else making complementary decisions. For example, a business owner’s decision to set up a factory, depends on the availability of workers with the right skills, of suppliers with the right parts and materials, of customers with the purchasing power and need, and on governments with the ability to install and maintain infrastructure.
Often, too, a decision that is fine for an individual is a problem if done for everyone else. For example, a government prints $10,000 new dollars and sends them to you: that’s great for you! But if everyone in the country gets $10,000 of newly-printed money, the result is rising prices and shrinking purchasing power for everyone.




What determines how well people can live and why do living standards rise?
Why is it so hard (or easy) for millions of people to find work?
Why does the financial system normally work really well? Why does it suddenly crash sometimes?
What drives changes in the purchasing power of my money?
Can society, through its government, come up with policies to manage the economy?

1.2 Three Graphs
The blue, solid line is the actual size of the economy of the United States since 1947. Notice the periods when the economy shrank, but also notice the long-term pattern of growth around potential output, the dashed red line.

title: 1  The Macroeconomic Perspective
text:
1.3 The Habits of the Macroeconomist
To think like a macroeconomist is to

Follow Connections. If you spend less at the local restaurant, what happens to the restaurant workers’ income? Everyone’s spending is someone else’s income; people save so that others may invest in new capital; pumping money into the economy increases spending but can also lead to inflation.
Add It Up. If everyone spends less, what happens to everyone’s income? In Micro, one person’s spending doesn’t change the entire economy. In Macro, we aggregate, meaning that we add up: add up spending on all products, add up the incomes of workers and owners, add up the production of farmers, factories, and financial firms, add up everything that can be considered money.
Keep It Real. It’s not about the dollars you get paid – it’s about how much they can buy. It’s about how living standards change, how your material welfare changes. If your wages rise by 10% but prices rise by 11%, you are no richer. If a country produces 20 times more than another country but has 30 times more people, it’s not more prosperous.
Separate the Long and Short of It. A country is richer because of a long-term trend, as its economy grew over generations. But its people might have trouble finding work in any particular year due to temporary fluctuations around that trend. The distinction between short-run cycles and the long-run path is crucial to macroeconomics.
Cut It Some Slack. An economy can operate above its potential, or short of it. If the economy is producing less than its capacity, you see unemployment. Inflation typically picks up if the economy is operating above capacity.
Look at the Forest. “How is the economy doing?” is not the kind of question you can ask by just looking at one number. You need to look at the whole picture: GDP growth, inflation, and unemployment are the three big statistics, but even an accurate aggregate can conceal differences across households and communities.
Explain, Test, Repeat. It’s easy to tell a simple, memorable story. But the truth is often more interesting and more complex. Build a real explanation of the world around you, and then test it by asking, “if my explanation is true, then what would I observe?”

title: 1  The Macroeconomic Perspective
text:
1.4 Interpret the Data
Look back at Figure 1.1. Can output rise over a long time but fall over a shorter period?
Search the internet for this answer, and explain it in your own words: if unemployment is 5%, does that mean that 95% of the population is employed? Look at Figure 1.2 for last month’s unemployment rate.
Figure 1.3 shows that between June 2022 and December 2024, inflation fell from more than 9% to 2.6%. Does this mean that prices returned to where they started? Hint: the definition of inflation is “the growth rate of prices.”
Macroeconomists love graphs. But not because they explain anything. Graphs tell us what happened, but it is up to a good theory to explain why and how it happened. We need a causal mechanism and complementary evidence.
We also love variables like “GDP per capita,” which is the size of the economy divided by the population. But we know that a single variable can never be a complete answer to complicated questions like “are people better off?” So we want to measure economic performance, and we want to explain it, but we also want to evaluate it. Never confuse “up” with “good.”

title: 1  The Macroeconomic Perspective
text:
1.5 Think About It
Think about a situation in your life when a decision made sense if you only did it, but it was bad when everyone did it. Or a decision that you needed everyone else to do it for it to make sense for you.
Choose one dashboard measure, like GDP, unemployment, or inflation. What does it tell us, and what does it not tell us?

title: 1  The Macroeconomic Perspective
text:
1.6 Try It Yourself

Go to https://fred.stlouisfed.org/ and search for “real gdp per person.” You should find “Real gross domestic product per capita” pretty quickly. What do you think is the difference between this and what is plotted in Figure 1.1? What happened in 2008 and 2020? We are better off than people were in 1950 … how much better?
Go to FRED and search for PAYEMS. Click to open the graph. Then select only the last 5 Years by clicking on 5Y. And then click on Edit Graph at the top right. Change the Units to “Change, Thousands of Persons.” This graph shows you how many jobs are added every month in the United States. What do you think – is the US economy in good shape?
Compare this graph with Figure 1.2: how is payroll employment related to the unemployment rate?
Go to FRED and search for CPIAUCSL. This is the typical cost of living in an American City, rescaled so that everything is measured as a percentage of 1982-1984. (Don’t ask - no one really knows they picked why those years. I guess they just had to pick something.) When do prices go down in the United States – what do those gray bars mean? Which are some of the periods in which prices have risen faster?
Pro tip: in Edit Graph > Format, click on Log Scale Left. Then the slope of the line is the inflation rate. When did the US last experience a long period of high inflation?
This CPIAUSCL is different from the economic variable plotted in Figure 1.3. What’s the difference? You may have to do a little internet research.

Problem 1 is about living standards. Problem 2 is about our ability to find work. Problem 3 is about the purchasing power of our money.

title: 2  Living Standards and Productivity
text:
2.1 How does economic growth work?
Imagine living in your hometown, today, with only $10-$20/week to pay for rent, groceries, gas, food, education, clothing, medical care, and fun. That was the situation of the vast majority of humanity since the dawn of human history until relatively recently. In other words, everyone was not only poor, but miserably poor. Even the kings and queens didn’t have electricity, toilets, or the internet. Millions died from diseases that today we cure with soap and water.
This might be one of the most amazing graphs ever. For millennia, living standards barely changed. Then, somethings switched, and living standards have grown exponentially, for 200 years, in practically every country in the world.
Figure 2.1 shows GDP per capita, the average value of goods and services available to a person in the country (rather than GDP, the total size of the economy). Per capita is what we actually care about, because it determines our material living standards. Here’s a great comparison between the UK, the USA, and China.
England’s income per person grew at an average of 0.05 percent per year between 1250 and 1650, implying that GDP per capita would double every 1400 years. From 1650 to 1820, the average annual growth rate rose to 0.41 percent, reducing doubling time to only (!) 170 years. China’s growth rate between 1150 and 1968 was a negative 0.00031 percent, essentially flat for 800 years.
Starting in the early 1820s, something happened. Table 2.1 Western offshoots like the United States were growing faster than everyone else, at triple that “higher” English rate of the previous period, and sustained it. All other regions matched that growth rate after World War I, and especially after 1950. By 1980, you were disappointed if your country wasn’t growing at 2 percent. The world-average growth rate today is triple the nineteenth-century average. Instead of taking a lifetime for incomes to double, it only takes a generation. China’s real GDP per capita today is just a little over $19,000.
What is the explanation for these extraordinary patterns? How does an economy grow over time?
You are the ruler of your kingdom. The typical person enjoys approximately $1000/year (about $2.75/day) of goods and services. GDP per capita grows at about 0.1 percent a year, which means that it will double in approximately 693 years. Then, it starts growing at 1 percent a year, and now it doubles in 70 years.
You are the president of your country, where GDP per capita is $20,000. You are going to implement a policy that will increase the growth rate of real GDP per person from 2 to 4 percent. Compare the value of real GDP per person twenty years from now under each policy. (For context, between 1978 and 2011, US living standards grew at an annual average of 1.81 percent; Chinese living standards grew at an annual average of 8.8 percent.)
In the animation below, change the starting real GDP per capita and the average annual growth rate.
viewof startingGDP = Inputs.range([100, 150000], {
  value: 1000,
  step: 100,
  label: "Starting real GDP per capita ($)"
})

viewof growthPercent = Inputs.range([0, 15], {
  value: 0.1,
  step: 0.1,
  label: "Annual growth rate (%)"
})
startingYear = new Date().getFullYear()

growthRate = growthPercent / 100

yearsToDouble = growthRate > 0
  ? Math.log(2) / Math.log1p(growthRate)
  : null

projectionLength = yearsToDouble === null
  ? 50
  : Math.max(50, yearsToDouble)

dollarFormat = new Intl.NumberFormat("en-US", {
  style: "currency",
  currency: "USD",
  maximumFractionDigits: 0
})

doublingMessage = yearsToDouble === null
  ? "At 0% growth, GDP per capita stays constant."
  : "Real GDP per capita first reaches at least twice current value in "
    + Math.ceil((startingYear + yearsToDouble))
    + ", after " + yearsToDouble
    + " years."

projection = Array.from(
  {length: projectionLength + 1},
  (_, t) => ({
    year: startingYear + t,
    elapsed: t,
    gdp: startingGDP * Math.pow(1 + growthRate, t)
  })
)
doublingMessage







Inputs.table(projection, {
  columns: ["year", "elapsed", "gdp"],
  header: {
    year: "Year",
    elapsed: "Years elapsed",
    gdp: "Real GDP per capita"
  },
  format: {
    year: d => String(d),
    elapsed: d => String(d),
    gdp: d => dollarFormat.format(d)
  },
  rows: 15
})
How do we calculate the number of years for real GDP per capita to double? Suppose \(y\) starts at \(y_0\): for example, let’s say that real GDP per capita starts at $20,000. The value of \(y\) after one year, if it’s growing at \(r\), is \(y_1=y_0(1+r)\). After two years, it would be \(y_2=y_0(1+r)^2\). The value of \(y\) after \(t\) years, if it’s growing at \(r\), it will be \(y_t = y_0(1+r)^t\). When will \(y_t=2\times y_0\)? A little math will help. It turns out doubling time \(t\) is approximately \[t=\frac{72}{r\times100}\]so it is called the Rule of 72. Try it: how long will it take for your savings to double if they are growing at 6 percent?

title: 2  Living Standards and Productivity
text:
2.2 Reading
Read these short pieces before reading the rest of the chapter:

Max Roser (2026) How is life at different levels of GDP per capita? What is one outcome beyond possessions that tends to be better in richer countries?
OECD (2025) “OECD job markets remain resilient but population ageing will cause significant labour shortages and fiscal pressures.” How could population aging slow growth in output per person, and which responses work through employment rather than productivity?
Atsushi Iimi (2006) Botswana: Avoiding the Resource Curse. What besides diamonds helps explain Botswana’s success? Identify one limitation the author still acknowledges.
Diana Roy and Amelia Cheatham (2024) “Venezuela: The Rise and Fall of a Petrostate”. How could oil wealth weaken a country’s ability to produce other goods and services—and weaken the incentives for accountable government?

Material living standards concern access to goods and services. Is that the same as being happy, holy, or good? No, but sometimes we are interested in something basic like material productive capacity. In this chapter, we are interested in “price-adjusted output” also called “real GDP,” which we label with \(Y\). As a matter of fact, we care about the amount of goods and services available to people in a country, \(Y\), divided by how many people there are in the country, \(N\): \[
\frac{Y}{N}
\] which we call Real GDP per capita, or real GDP per person.

title: 2  Living Standards and Productivity
text:
2.3 Adam Smith’s Explanation
In 1776, a professor in Scotland published a book that would change the world. Adam Smith’s Wealth of Nations is not the only famous document that came out that year, but it’s pretty famous. He opens the book, basically, by giving us the key to the question of this chapter: why do some countries grow richer than others? His answer boils it down to two factors: (1) the effectiveness of labor, by which we mean output per worker, also known as average labor productivity, or real GDP divided by the number of people employed, \(Y/E\), and (2) the proportion engaged in useful labor, which is the employment-to-population ratio, \(E\) divided by \(N\).
Let’s do a little math. Divide both sides of the real-GDP-per-capita fraction by \(E\). Because we are dividing both sides by the same number, it is still the old \(Y/N\) in new clothes. Then rearrange, which basically means we have “decomposed” real GDP per capita into its constituent parts. \[
\frac{Y / E}{N / E} = \frac{Y}{E}\times \frac{E}{N}
\] Just to keep the notation compact, let’s say that \(y\) is real GDP per person, \(ALP\) is average labor productivity, and \(EMR\) is the employment-population ratio. Then we can say \[
y=ALP \times EPR
\tag{2.1}\]

2.3.1 Alternative Explanations: some wrong turns
Smith’s was not the first theory of riches-versus-poverty. Often people think that having a lot of natural resources is the key to riches. More resources means that you have more with which to produce, so you can make more GDP for each person.
But as the readings suggest, it’s not about the resources you have, but about what you do with them. There’s such a thing as having too much unearned wealth. Resource rents can be captured by kings, war lords, and corporate titans, easy streams of public revenue can be mismanaged, and dependence creates vulnerability.
In Figure 2.2 you can see that the countries with the most natural resources rents are not necessarily very rich: in fact, some of the world’s richest countries earn only a small fraction of their income out of natural resources. Hover over the following graph to identify each country. The bubble identifies the size of the population; the colors identify continents.






Figure 2.2



Really? How do resource-poor countries get around their scarcity? They trade. Long ago, countries figured out that they could get access to other country’s resources by producing what those countries needed, in exchange for the resources they lacked. For example, country P could by the raw materials from country R, manufacture them into something desirable, and sell it back to country R.
So far, that’s true. But then history took a wrong turn by thinking that it was all about trade: specifically, a trade surplus. Mercantilists thought that the wealth of nations is the accumulation of gold and silver, and that to accumulate precious metals you need more exports than imports: favorable trade balances became central national objectives; trade deficits were thought to be the source and symptom of national weakness.
To make trade deficits go away, countries used tariffs to make foreign goods more expensive. But you can see in Figure 2.3 that, if anything, richer countries have lower average tariffs.






Figure 2.3



Tariffs protect domestic producers from foreign competition, and domestic consumers pay the higher price. So mercantilism is an attractive policy to kings, warlords, and corporate titans, but not the key to long term economic growth.
In short: neither abundant natural resources nor high tariffs explain differences in living standards.


2.3.2 Back to Smith’s explanations
Let’s go back to Adam Smith’s two explanations for economic prosperity: average labor productivity and the employment-to-population ratio. What could cause \(EPR\) to rise?

Fewer people go to school. Rather than going to college, people start to work at four, raising the proportion of workers in the population.
People retire later, or live shorter lives, so that they spend fewer years in retirement.
There are more young people working.

It’s OK if you think that there must be something wrong with this explanation. Doesn’t “high living standards” mean the ability to retire early? Doesn’t more education correlate with higher income?






Figure 2.4



Do you see any patterns in Figure 2.4? The countries with the highest \(EPR\) are countries that are quite poor. It makes sense: if you are very poor, you can’t afford to retire and you can’t afford to go to school. But not going to school makes you poor: the lowest \(EPR\) is in countries that are very poor. In the middle, you have very rich countries and very poor countries: USA and Congo have approximately the same \(EPR\). It would seem that \(EPR\) is not a very good predictor of \(y\). Do you have an alternative theory?

title: 2  Living Standards and Productivity
section: 2.4 Average Labor Productivity as the Key Determinant of Living Standards
text:
2.4 Average Labor Productivity as the Key Determinant of Living Standards

The single most important determinant of long-term living standards is average labor productivity.

Figure 2.5 shows you the incredibly strong correlation between worker productivity and living standards.






Figure 2.5



Figure 2.6 shows you three related, and very important, facts. First, the productivity of labor has been increasing, by a lot, in nearly every country. Second, workers in some countries are much more productive than in others, and their productivity grows at radically different rates. China’s average worker produced $0.50/hour in 1952 and today produces $17.7/hour; in South Korea, productivity has gone from $1.70/hour to $53.6/hour. The rate of productivity increase is nothing short of fantastic for some countries … but pretty pedestrian for others.
And third, you can see that, although productivity is key, it is not the only explanation: German workers are nearly as productive as American workers, but German real GDP per capita is only 80% of America’s: the difference is due to Germany’s smaller employment-to-population ratio.






Figure 2.6



This raises the next question. What determines average labor productivity? We will consider three related factors in the next three chapters:

The accumulation of capital
The progress of technology
Institutions and the structure of society
